post_text: Across the Soviet Union, the exchange "Where?" "In Karaganda!" was a punchline about the middle of nowhere. The city, on the steppe of central Kazakhstan, now has a monument to the joke and about half a million residents. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ Coal. It was found here in the 1800s, credited to a shepherd, though who found it first is disputed. In the late 1920s Soviet planners drafted a dozen mines and a city to serve them. They also set up Karlag, a prison camp network built to supply the mines with slave labor.

3/ Deportees built it too. Two or three families shared a dugout, heated with weeds and dried dung. Cold, scurvy and typhus caused mass deaths in 1931–33. By the 1940s up to 70% of residents were ethnic Germans. Over 100,000 people have since emigrated to Germany.

4/ Coal still keeps it going. 8 mines remain of up to 26 in Soviet times, and the city's water comes by canal from the Irtysh River, more than 400 km away. Methane makes the work deadly. In October 2023 a fire at the Kostenko mine killed at least 32 people.

post_text: Ghadames gets 73 mm of rain a year and July highs around 41°C, and for most of its history it drank from a single spring. It's an oasis town in northwestern Libya, near the Algerian and Tunisian borders. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ The reason is a spring, Ain al-Faras: 'the only source of life,' one study calls it. Its water was split among seven clans on a strict schedule, timed by a pierced cup called the gâddous, via five canals proportioned 1:3:9:27:81. The community still manages it.

3/ Water made it a stop; trade made it rich. From Arab rule until the 19th century it sat at a junction of caravan routes. Caravans from the south brought slaves, gold, ivory and ostrich feathers, and its traders reached Timbuktu. When that trade vanished, the town declined.

4/ The old mud town is almost fully roofed over: supplies downstairs, families above covered alleys, linked rooftops reserved for women as their own streets. People moved to new houses outside. No one lives in it year-round, but many return in summer to escape the heat.

post_text: Its Inuktitut name, Aujuittuq, means "place that never thaws." The average yearly temperature is −16.5 °C. Grise Fiord, on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut, is Canada's northernmost civilian community, with 144 people at the 2021 census. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ Because Canada put them there. In 1953 the government moved Inuit families from Inukjuak (then Port Harrison), Quebec, to the High Arctic. They were promised homes and plentiful caribou. They found no buildings and were told to take one caribou per family per year.

3/ They were told they could go home if they wished, after one year or after two or three, depending on the account. The offer was later withdrawn. The motive is disputed: the government calls the move humanitarian; many argue it was about Cold War Arctic sovereignty.

4/ Families learned the beluga routes and stayed. In 2010 Canada apologized. In Grise Fiord, a statue of a woman, a boy and a husky gazes toward Resolute Bay, where other relocated families were sent. In Resolute, a statue of a lone man looks back.

post_text: In July 1983 the air here fell to −89.2 °C, the lowest temperature ever reliably measured on Earth. The air holds as little oxygen as the top of Mount Elbrus. Vostok Station is a Russian base 3,488 m up on the East Antarctic ice sheet. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ The Soviets built it in 1957 because of what lay nearby: the South Geomagnetic Pole, where Earth's magnetic axis meets the surface, a good spot to study the ionosphere and magnetic storms. But magnetic poles wander. By 1996 it was about 100 km away.

3/ The real prize was underneath. A core drilled with the French stopped at 3,623 m in 1996 and held 420,000 years of climate history, across four previous glacial periods. Below it lies Lake Vostok, 14,000 sq km, under about 4 km of ice. Drillers reached it in 2012.

4/ Newcomers lose 5–10 kg in their first month. Rescue is impossible eight months a year. In April 1982 the generator shed burned and chief mechanic Aleksei Karpenko died trying to save it. The rest wintered huddled in a small hut, heated by wicks dipped in diesel.

post_text: A Low German-speaking Mennonite town in the Belize jungle, reached partly by a hand-cranked ferry, produces the country's only commercial milk and pumps its only oil. Spanish Lookout, Cayo District, Belize. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ They had moved before. Dutch-Russian Mennonites, they settled in Canada in the 1870s and Mexico in 1948. Then Mexico couldn't promise their sons draft exemption and wouldn't sell them much more land. In March 1958 the first group landed in British Honduras.

3/ George Price wanted Belize less dependent on its neighbours. The deal: their own churches and schools, with their own teachers, in exchange for BZ$500,000 of investment and paying every cost of settling. They started in jungle, with a tree as the church.

4/ The settlement, 3,108 people in 2022, now has Western Dairies, Belize's only commercial milk producer, and reportedly its largest chicken and egg suppliers. It also has Belize's only oilfield, past its 5,000-barrel-a-day peak and nearing its economic limit around 2030.

post_text: In 1973 a volcano erupted on Heimaey, a small island off Iceland's south coast. Lava crushed half the town and headed for the harbour. Everyone left overnight, mostly on fishing boats. Then many came back. Why do people live here?
thread_parts: 2/ The harbour. Cliffs shelter it, and extremely rich fishing grounds lie minutes away, beside cliffs full of nesting seabirds. Tradition says Herjólfur Bárðarson settled here about 900; a 1971 dig found settlement nearly a century earlier.

3/ It still pays. The Westman Islands hold about 2% of Iceland's people and land 15% of its catch. Fish come ashore and into processing almost immediately. The largest employer, Vinnslustöðin, was started on the last day of 1946 by 105 local fishermen.

4/ So in 1973 they fought for the harbour, spraying the lava with six million tons of seawater until it hardened and turned aside. It worked. One man died. Islanders came back, dug out their houses and heated them with the lava. The island grew from 11.2 to 13.44 km².
